title: Stage 5: Chirp at 1M users
scopeHtml: Scope: async work, queue choice SQS vs RabbitMQ vs Kafka, workers, idempotency, retries, DLQ, image pipeline. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Load and goal
notes.html:
Stage 5: about 1,000,000 users. Goal: move slow, failure-prone, bursty work out of the request path into queues and workers, so requests stay fast and one broken dependency cannot break posting.

Worked example. 1M users, 30% DAU = 300,000 DAU. Timeline reads: 300k x 20 = 6M/day = about 70/s average, peak 5x = 350/s (hits mostly cache). Posts: 1.5 per DAU = 450k/day = about 5 writes/s average, 25/s at peak. Images: 20% of posts = 90k uploads/day, 3 variants each = 270k resize outputs/day. Resize costs about 150 ms CPU each with libvips on a vCPU, so 90k x 0.45 s = 40,500 CPU-seconds a day = about 0.5 cores average, but bursts at peak are 10x. Notifications: each post notifies on average 5 followers who want pushes = 2.25M notifications/day = 26/s average, bursts of thousands when a celebrity posts.

Industry examples. Instagram uses Celery/RabbitMQ-style task queues; Pinterest uses Kafka; Uber and Netflix use Kafka for event streams; Shopify runs huge Sidekiq (Redis) queues; Dropbox uses queues for thumbnailing.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant takes your order at the counter (fast), gives a ticket number and the kitchen works the tickets. The counter is never blocked by the grill.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a queue when the user needs the answer in the same request (for example "is this username free?").
  • Not saying what the user sees while work is pending (a "processing" state).

Common interview traps.

  • Visibility timeout shorter than job time: the job is delivered twice while still running. Set it to a multiple of the typical time, or extend it with a heartbeat.
  • Short polling with many workers: lots of empty receives and cost.

notes.title: Decision and why
notes.html:
Decision 1: which work is async. Rule: if the user does not need the result to receive their response, queue it. Async: image resize, push/email notifications, search indexing, counters flushing, follower-count rebuilds. Sync: creating the post row (user must see it), authentication, reading.

Decision 2: upload directly to S3. The API does not touch image bytes. A 4 MB upload through the API occupies a thread and bandwidth; a presigned URL moves that to S3. The API only stores the media_key and a status = PROCESSING.

Decision 3: transactional hand-off ("outbox"). If you save a post and then publish to the queue, a crash between the two loses the job. Fix: write an outbox row in the same DB transaction, and a relay publishes it to the queue and marks it sent. Result: at-least-once delivery without a distributed transaction.

CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  topic TEXT NOT NULL,
  payload JSONB NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
  sent_at TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX outbox_unsent ON outbox (id) WHERE sent_at IS NULL;

Decision 4: idempotent consumers. Queues deliver at-least-once, so a job can run twice. Each job has a stable job_id (for example media:{post_id}:{variant}). The worker inserts into processed_jobs(job_id PRIMARY KEY) first; if it conflicts, it acks and skips. Operations are also naturally idempotent: output keys are deterministic (img/{hash}/{size}.webp), so rewriting the same object is harmless.

Decision 5: retries with backoff and a DLQ. Transient failure (timeout, 503): retry with exponential backoff plus jitter (1 s, 2 s, 4 s ... capped at 60 s) using ChangeMessageVisibility. Permanent failure (corrupt image): do not retry; send to DLQ immediately. After maxReceiveCount=5, the message lands in the DLQ; an alarm fires when DLQ depth above 0; a human inspects, fixes, and "redrives" them.

Decision 6: backpressure. Workers pull; queue depth is the shock absorber. Alarm on queue age (ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage above 120 s) rather than depth alone.

Industry examples. Stripe makes every API write idempotent with an Idempotency-Key header; Debezium and the "transactional outbox" pattern are standard in Uber and Shopify style event systems; AWS Lambda/SQS integrations rely on DLQ and partial batch failure responses.

Everyday analogy. A parcel hub: parcels arrive in bursts, workers take them off the belt; a damaged parcel goes into a "problem" bin instead of blocking the belt.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming "exactly once" delivery. The honest answer is at-least-once plus idempotent processing.
  • Unbounded retries with no DLQ: a poison message loops forever and burns money.

notes.title: Alternatives (branches)
notes.html:
Branch 5A: Amazon SQS (chosen for Stage 5)

Fully managed queue; standard queue = at-least-once, best-effort ordering, nearly unlimited throughput; FIFO queue = ordering per message group, 300 messages/s (3,000 with batching, higher with high-throughput mode).

  • Pros: zero ops, scales automatically, built-in DLQ and visibility timeout, about $0.40 per million requests.
  • Cons: no replay of consumed messages, no consumer groups (one logical consumer per queue; for fan-out use SNS to SQS), 256 KB message cap (store a pointer, not the image).
  • Fit: job queues, background tasks. Exactly Stage 5's need.

Branch 5B: RabbitMQ

Broker with exchanges (direct, topic, fanout), acknowledgements, priorities, TTL, plugin ecosystem.

  • Pros: rich routing, priority queues, low latency (sub-millisecond), request/reply patterns, good on-prem.
  • Cons: you operate it (cluster of 3 m6g.large, quorum queues, disk alarms); throughput tens of thousands of messages/s per node, not millions; no long retention or replay (classic queues); big backlog hurts memory.
  • Fit: complex routing, small team that wants per-message priorities. Rejected here for ops cost.

Branch 5C: Apache Kafka

Distributed append-only log with partitions and consumer groups; consumers track offsets.

  • Pros: huge throughput (hundreds of MB/s), ordering within a partition, replay (retention 7 days or forever), many independent consumers read the same stream, exactly-once semantics within Kafka with transactions.
  • Cons: heavy ops (3 brokers m6g.xlarge, ZooKeeper-free KRaft, partition planning, rebalance pain, or MSK at about $0.20 per broker-hour plus storage); no per-message retry or DLQ built in (you build retry topics); partitions cannot easily be reduced.
  • Fit: event streams, replay, many consumers. Not needed for simple jobs at 25 posts/s. Expected later: a post.created topic with, for example, 12 partitions keyed by author_id to feed fan-out and search indexing at higher scale.
SQS RabbitMQ Kafka
Model queue broker with routing partitioned log
Replay no no yes
Ordering FIFO optional per queue per partition
Retry / DLQ built in built in (dead-letter exchange) build yourself
Ops none medium high (or MSK cost)
Throughput very high, elastic tens of thousands/s per node millions/s
Chirp Stage 5 chosen rejected later, for event streaming

Config examples for the alternatives:

# Kafka topic for later stages
topic: post.created
partitions: 12
replication.factor: 3
min.insync.replicas: 2
retention.ms: 604800000   # 7 days
producer: { acks: all, enable.idempotence: true, compression.type: lz4 }
# RabbitMQ quorum queue with dead lettering
rabbitmqadmin declare queue name=media durable=true \
  arguments='{"x-queue-type":"quorum","x-dead-letter-exchange":"dlx","x-delivery-limit":5}'

Industry examples. LinkedIn built Kafka for activity streams; Uber and Netflix use it as the event backbone; many Rails/Django shops use SQS/Sidekiq/Celery for background jobs; RabbitMQ is common in banking and telecom for routing.

Everyday analogy. SQS is a ticket line where each ticket is handled once and thrown away; Kafka is a newspaper archive many readers can read from any day; RabbitMQ is a post office that sorts letters to different pigeonholes.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing Kafka for every async need. It is a log, not a task queue.
  • Ignoring that SQS standard may deliver out of order.

notes.title: What breaks next
notes.html:
1. Timeline reads are still pull-based: every timeline miss runs a join over followees. Celebrities with millions of followers make fan-out a new problem. Metric: timeline cache miss ratio and primary CPU.
  2. Primary DB writes and size: 500 GB and 25 writes/s is fine, but tables like posts and notifications grow by hundreds of millions of rows; vacuum, index builds and backups get slow.
  3. Search in Postgres (tsvector) is straining; needs a dedicated search engine.
  4. Single region: an outage takes everything down.
  5. Operational complexity: more moving parts (queues, workers, DLQs) need dashboards and on-call.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing the queue fixes the DB bottleneck. It smooths bursts; it does not add DB capacity.

notes.title: LLD view
notes.html:
New concepts in code: producer, consumer, idempotency guard, outbox relay.

PostService.create()
   BEGIN tx
     INSERT posts (status=PROCESSING)
     INSERT outbox(topic=media, payload={post_id,key})
   COMMIT
OutboxRelay (every 500 ms): SELECT ... WHERE sent_at IS NULL FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED -> sqs.send -> mark sent

MediaWorker.handle(msg):
   if !idempotency.tryClaim(jobId) return ack
   download raw -> resize x3 -> upload variants -> UPDATE posts SET status=READY
   on transient error -> change visibility (backoff) ; on permanent -> DLQ
interface JobHandler { fun handle(job: Job) }

class IdempotentHandler(private val inner: JobHandler, private val jdbc: JdbcTemplate) : JobHandler {
    override fun handle(job: Job) {
        val first = jdbc.update(
            "INSERT INTO processed_jobs(job_id) VALUES (?) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING", job.id) == 1
        if (first) inner.handle(job)       // duplicate deliveries become no-ops
    }
}

A caveat: claim and effect should be in the same transaction when the effect is a DB write; otherwise a crash after claiming leaves the job lost. For S3 output, deterministic keys already make reruns safe, so claim after success.

Class view:

JobQueue <<interface>> <- SqsJobQueue
JobHandler <<interface>> <- MediaHandler, NotifyHandler, IndexHandler
IdempotentHandler (decorator), RetryPolicy(backoff, jitter, max), OutboxRelay

Industry examples. Sidekiq, Celery and Spring Cloud Stream expose the same shapes: producer, handler, retry policy, dead letter.

Common interview traps.

  • Acking the message before the work finishes; a crash loses the job.
  • Making handlers depend on message order when the queue gives no order guarantee.

notes.title: Decision gravity
notes.html:
Decision Gravity Why
SQS as the job queue Reversible Behind JobQueue interface; swap to RabbitMQ/Kafka by adapter
Moving to Kafka later One-way-ish Partition keys and consumer semantics leak into design; plan the key (author_id) carefully
At-least-once + idempotency One-way discipline Every consumer must stay idempotent forever
Outbox table Reversible Can be replaced by CDC (Debezium) later
Direct-to-S3 uploads Reversible Client contract (presigned flow) is the sticky part
Image variants / WebP Mostly reversible Reprocessing old media is a costly batch job; keep originals
Retention and DLQ policy Reversible Config
Public API returns status: PROCESSING One-way for clients Mobile apps must handle the pending state

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting that adding a new image size later means reprocessing every stored original.

notes.title: Concepts learned
notes.html:
• Sync vs async; what must stay in the request path.
  • Queue vs log; SQS vs RabbitMQ vs Kafka (5A/5B/5C).
  • At-least-once delivery, idempotency keys, deduplication tables.
  • Retries with exponential backoff and jitter; poison messages; DLQ and redrive.
  • Visibility timeout, long polling, backpressure, queue age as an alarm.
  • Transactional outbox; presigned direct uploads; autoscaling workers on queue depth.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing "idempotent" with "only runs once".

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Stage 5 (about 1M users): API on 6 c6i.xlarge, DB db.r6g.2xlarge + 2 replicas, Redis cache.m6g.xlarge, SQS queues with DLQs and 2 to 40 autoscaled workers; about $8,700 per month.
  • Queue anything the user does not wait for: image resize (3 WebP variants), notifications, search indexing, counter flushes.
  • Queue choice: SQS chosen (managed, DLQ, cheap); RabbitMQ for complex routing; Kafka for replayable streams, expected later keyed by author_id.
  • Safety: transactional outbox, at-least-once delivery, idempotent handlers, retry with backoff and jitter, maxReceiveCount=5, DLQ alarm.
  • Handoff to Stage 6+: pull-based timelines, a single write primary, Postgres search and single region are the remaining limits.
